In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker,﴾ ﴿who gathers wealth and counts it,﴾ ﴿thinking that his wealth will make him immortal.﴾ ﴿No! He will surely be thrown into the Crushing Fire.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing Fire is?﴾ ﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled,﴾ ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ ﴿It is closed down upon them,﴾ ﴿in extended columns.﴾

(p-510) Al-Hutama (the Crusher): its origin is an adjective from their saying "rajul hutama," meaning a great eater. The rajaz poet said:

"The night has wrapped it with the driver of the hutam."

Another said:

"Indeed we crushed Mus'ab with the staff, on the day we broke his nose, so that he would become angry."

It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, or al-As ibn Wa'il, or Jamil ibn Ma'mar, or al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, or Umayya ibn Khalaf; there are opinions. I have mentioned him, although the wording is general, because Allah, glory be to Him, followed up on his attributes and the report about him until it was understood that He was pointing to a specific person. Similarly His saying in Surah Nun: ﴿And do not obey every constant swearer, despicable one﴾ [al-Qalam: 10]. He followed up with attributes until it was known that He meant a specific person. The discussion of al-Humaza was already given in Surah Nun, and of al-Lumaza in Surah Bara'a. Its verb is from the intensive patterns, like nawama (one who sleeps much), 'uyaba (one who finds fault much), suhara (one who practices magic much), and dahika (one who laughs much). Ziyad al-A'jam said:

"You show me affection when you meet me, falsely, and when I am absent you are the one who points and mocks."

The majority read al-Humaza and al-Lumaza with a fatha on the mim in both; the rest with a sukun. It means the jester who brings forth jokes, who insults, points, and mocks. (Alladhi) is an apposition, or in the accusative as a means of censure. Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Amir, and the two brothers read "jam'" with a doubled mim; the rest of the seven read it with lightening. The majority read "wa-'addadahu" with a doubled first dal, meaning: he counted it and guarded it. It was said: he made it a reserve against the vicissitudes of time. Al-Hasan and al-Kalbi read both lightened, meaning he gathered wealth and kept its count. It was said: and a number of his clan. It was said: and he counted it, leaving off the assimilation, like His saying:

"Indeed I am generous to people even if they are stingy."

(Akhladahu) means: he kept him alive, for by it is the sustenance of his life and its preservation throughout his lifespan. Al-Zamakhshari said: wealth lengthened his hope and gave him far-reaching wishes, until, through excessive heedlessness and long hope, he thinks that wealth has left him to live forever in this world and never die. It was said: al-Akhnas had four thousand dinars, and it was said ten thousand dinars. (Kalla) is a rebuke to him for his assumption. The majority read "la-yunbadhanna" with a singular pronoun. Ali and al-Hasan, in one report from him, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Harun from Abu Amr read "la-yunbadhani" with the dual alif, referring to the scorner and his wealth. Also from al-Hasan: "la-yunbadhdhu" with a damma on the dhal, meaning he and his helpers. From Abu Amr: "la-yanbudhannahu." The majority read "fi al-Hutama" and "wa-ma adraka ma al-Hutama"; Zayd ibn Ali read "fi al-Hatima" and "wa-ma adraka ma al-Hatima," and it is the fire whose nature is to crush everything cast into it. Al-Dahhak said: al-Hutama is the fourth level of the Fire. Al-Kalbi said: the sixth stratum of Jahannam. Al-Qushayri reported from him that it is the second level; and from him also: the second gate. ﴿The Fire of Allah﴾, that is, it is the Hutama, ﴿which rises over the hearts.﴾ The hearts are mentioned because they are the most delicate part of the body and the most sensitive to pain from the slightest harm. The fire's rising over them means that it overtops them and encloses them, though it overtops the unbelievers throughout their bodies; but He drew attention to the noblest part, because it is the seat of beliefs. The apparent meaning is that it is the fire of the Hereafter, since they despair of leaving, with the doors closed upon them and the columns extended, all of which is a sign of eternal abiding without end. The apparent meaning is that it is the fire of the Hereafter, since they despair of leaving, with the doors closed upon them and the columns extended, all of which is a sign of eternal abiding without end. Qatada said: we were told that they are columns with which they are tormented in the Fire. Abu Salih said: they are shackles. And Allah knows best.
